nodes.name: Zhengtuo Zhao
nodes.subtitle: UT Austin PhD · Rice postdoc · StairMed
nodes.summary: Biomedical engineering researcher and StairMed co-founder. His doctorate was at UT Austin (2015–2019); Rice documented his postdoctoral work in 2020.

nodes.name: Chong Xie
nodes.subtitle: Xie laboratory · neural interfaces
nodes.summary: Neural-interface researcher whose lab alumni roster includes Zhengtuo Zhao. Corresponding author of the 2017 nanoelectronic-thread study.

nodes.name: UT Austin
nodes.subtitle: Doctoral training · 2015–2019
nodes.summary: Zhao’s institutional biography identifies UT Austin as his doctoral institution. The 2017 NET paper also lists UT Austin affiliations for Zhao, Luan and Xie.

nodes.name: Rice University
nodes.subtitle: Postdoctoral research · documented 2020
nodes.summary: Rice reported Zhao’s postdoctoral work in May 2020. His biography lists a broader UT Austin/Rice postdoc period without specifying the split between institutions.

nodes.name: StairMed
nodes.subtitle: Shanghai · established August 2021
nodes.summary: A neural-interface company co-founded by Zhengtuo Zhao and Xue Li. A 2026 human recording study documents the use of its recording hardware.

nodes.name: Nanoelectronic threads (NET)
nodes.subtitle: Ultraflexible penetrating probes · 2017
nodes.summary: Nanoelectronic threads aim to reduce mechanical mismatch with neural tissue. The original paper and later fabrication studies establish a traceable research thread.

nodes.name: MERF array
nodes.subtitle: Chronic nonhuman-primate recordings
nodes.summary: The MERF array adapts NET fabrication with changes to materials, electrode configuration and packaging for nonhuman-primate recordings.

nodes.name: Human uFINE system
nodes.subtitle: Temporary intraoperative recordings
nodes.summary: An ultraflexible human recording system whose paper extends earlier MERF fabrication and assembly methods and names StairMed recording hardware.

nodes.name: Utah intracortical array
nodes.subtitle: Device family · 1992
nodes.summary: The selected University of Utah paper describes a glass-isolated 10 × 10 bed of 100 silicon needles. Later human systems use specific wired configurations.

nodes.name: BrainGate human demonstration
nodes.subtitle: Research system · 2006
nodes.summary: A participant with tetraplegia controlled a cursor and external devices through a motor-cortex microelectrode array and decoder.

nodes.name: BrainGate2 research program
nodes.subtitle: Research program · 2009
nodes.summary: Academic continuation of BrainGate research. A 2012 study demonstrated robotic reach and grasp using implanted motor-cortex recordings.

nodes.name: Blackrock Neurotech
nodes.subtitle: Manufacturer · 2008
nodes.summary: Blackrock Microsystems, now Blackrock Neurotech, appears as a manufacturer in the BrainGate device history and later experimental methods.

nodes.name: Neuropixels 1.0
nodes.subtitle: Recording platform · 2017
nodes.summary: The Jun et al. collaboration integrated a dense shank and on-chip signal processing: 960 selectable sites and 384 simultaneous recording channels per probe.

nodes.name: Neuropixels 2.0
nodes.subtitle: Recording platform · 2021
nodes.summary: Miniaturized single- and four-shank probes combine denser site geometry with motion-correction methods for chronic recordings. Each probe has 384 simultaneous channels.

nodes.name: Neuropixels Ultra
nodes.subtitle: Platform variant · 2025
nodes.summary: An ultra-dense NP 1.0 platform variant samples extracellular electrical footprints using 5 × 5 µm sites at 6 µm pitch; selectable version: 6,144 sites, 384 simultaneous channels.

nodes.name: Cortical-surface ECoG
nodes.subtitle: Measurement method
nodes.summary: Contacts on the cortical surface record population-level electrical signals. Leuthardt et al. demonstrated online cursor control in four epilepsy-monitoring participants in 2004.

nodes.name: Precision thin-film cortical arrays
nodes.subtitle: Research platform · 2025
nodes.summary: Flexible subdural thin films connect through cables to external headstages. The paper evaluates implantation, neural recording, decoding, and stimulation.

nodes.name: BISC wireless µECoG chip
nodes.subtitle: Research platform · 2025
nodes.summary: A flexible 50-µm CMOS substrate integrates cortical-surface electrodes, electronics, wireless power, and telemetry: 65,536 sites with up to 1,024 selectable simultaneous channels.

nodes.name: Xue Li
nodes.subtitle: Xie lab alumnus · StairMed co-founder
nodes.summary: Xie’s lab lists Xue Li as a former PhD student. The human uFINE paper identifies Li and Zhengtuo Zhao as StairMed founders.

nodes.name: MIT
nodes.subtitle: Electrical engineering & computer science
nodes.summary: Rapoport earned his EECS PhD at MIT in 2011. This educational link is separate from his later company founding roles.

nodes.name: Benjamin Rapoport
nodes.subtitle: Neurosurgeon · electrical engineer
nodes.summary: Neurosurgeon and electrical engineer; MIT EECS PhD 2011, Harvard/HST MD 2013. Precision co-founder and Chief Science Officer.

nodes.name: Neuralink
nodes.subtitle: BCI company · founded 2016
nodes.summary: A BCI company that counts Rapoport among its co-founders. The shared person is the documented connection to Precision.

nodes.name: Precision Neuroscience
nodes.subtitle: Cortical-surface interfaces
nodes.summary: Rapoport is a co-founder. Its thin-film cortical arrays offer another route to recording at the brain surface.

nodes.name: Robinson Lab
nodes.subtitle: Rice University · neuroengineering
nodes.summary: Rice explicitly describes Motif as a startup spun out of Jacob Robinson’s lab. Its neuromodulation work includes miniature brain stimulators.

nodes.name: Motif Neurotech
nodes.subtitle: Miniature brain stimulation
nodes.summary: A company spun out of Robinson’s Rice lab. The cited university account concerns stimulation, with university and clinical collaborators.

nodes.name: University of Melbourne
nodes.subtitle: Multi-institution Stentrode development
nodes.summary: University investigators developed Stentrode with Synchron, Royal Melbourne Hospital, the Florey Institute and Monash collaborators.

nodes.name: Thomas Oxley
nodes.subtitle: Neurologist · Synchron co-founder
nodes.summary: University of Melbourne researcher and Synchron co-founder; Nicholas Opie is also explicitly identified as co-founder.

nodes.name: Synchron
nodes.subtitle: Endovascular BCI
nodes.summary: A company co-founded by Thomas Oxley and Nicholas Opie in 2012, with Stentrode developed through a multi-institution collaboration.

nodes.name: Richard Normann
nodes.subtitle: Utah Array development
nodes.summary: University of Utah professor emeritus credited with development of the Utah Electrode Array.

nodes.name: University of Utah
nodes.subtitle: Neural-interface research & licensing
nodes.summary: The institution where Normann developed the Utah Array. University accounts separately document technology licensed to Blackrock.

nodes.name: Xie Lab
nodes.subtitle: Rice University · neural interfaces
nodes.summary: A neural-interface laboratory led by Chong Xie, with an alumni roster documenting trainees including Zhengtuo Zhao and Xue Li. The current Rice affiliation does not relocate earlier UT Austin research.

nodes.name: Nicholas Opie
nodes.subtitle: Engineer · Synchron co-founder
nodes.summary: An engineer and Synchron co-founder named alongside Thomas Oxley in Melbourne’s commercialization account.

nodes.name: Stentrode
nodes.subtitle: Endovascular neural recording
nodes.summary: A stent-like recording interface positioned inside a blood vessel near motor cortex. It approaches neural recording through the vasculature.

edges.label: fabrication method adapted by
edges.detail: The MERF paper explicitly adapts NET's multilayer planar fabrication method, citing Luan et al. 2017. It describes replacing SU-8 with polyimide, changing the adhesion layer and repositioning/adding recording sites.
edges.limit: This is an author-stated technical adaptation, not an inferred similarity or licensing relationship.

sources.title: An Ultraflexible Electrode Array for Large-Scale Chronic Recording in the Nonhuman Primate Brain

edges.label: fabrication and assembly methods extended by
edges.detail: The uFINE Methods cite Tian et al. 2023 for prior fabrication and assembly, and describe improvements in tensile strength and medical-grade assembly materials.
edges.limit: The prior array is named MERF in its 2023 paper; avoid renaming it uFINE retroactively.

edges.label: provided recording hardware used in
edges.detail: The Methods identify StairMed headstages, data cable and StairPlex recording system used with the human uFINE array.
edges.limit: This study used temporary intraoperative recordings. It does not establish that this array is identical to StairMed's chronic wireless clinical implant.

edges.limit: Authorship identifies research contribution, not sole invention or patent ownership.

edges.label: uses a Utah-derived array
edges.detail: The 2006 paper reports a 96-microelectrode motor-cortex interface. The later BrainGate paper explicitly traces the system's silicon array to the University of Utah device, citing Jones et al. 1992.
edges.limit: The array is one component of a complete system with acquisition and decoding. Original 100-needle geometry and 96 recorded connections are different denominators.

edges.limit: This is research-program continuity, not evidence that every component was redesigned or that the system received marketing approval.

edges.label: uses Blackrock arrays and acquisition
edges.detail: The study's Methods identify a 96-channel Blackrock array in participant T2 and Cerebus Central acquisition software from Blackrock Microsystems.
edges.limit: A study-specific hardware relationship; BrainGate2 is an academic research program, not another name for Blackrock.

edges.detail: Blackrock's product page identifies the Utah Array as an array manufactured by Blackrock Neurotech.

edges.label: developed into
edges.detail: The NP 2.0 successor miniaturizes the platform. The developers compare NP 2.0 directly with NP 1.0: a smaller package, 15-µm vertical site spacing, aligned columns, and motion correction. Available sites increase to 1,280 on one shank or 5,120 across four.
edges.limit: The versions retain 384 simultaneous channels per probe. Four-shank total sites are not a same-geometry successor metric for a single shank.

sources.title: Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings

edges.label: platform used for
edges.detail: The Ultra paper states that shank dimensions, probe base, and mechanical characteristics match NP 1.0; its Materials availability section names the hardware Neuropixels 1.0 HD.
edges.limit: Ultra is not documented here as a successor descended from NP 2.0. Its 6,144-site count describes the selectable version; the paper also uses a fixed-site version.

sources.title: Ultra-high-density Neuropixels probes improve detection and identification in neuronal recordings

edges.label: coverage vs. density
edges.detail: NP 2.0 emphasizes chronic tracking and one/four-shank coverage; Ultra emphasizes densely sampled electrical footprints. Both papers specify 384 simultaneous channels per probe.
edges.limit: This pairing is an editorial technical comparison, not a historical-descent claim or a head-to-head clinical performance test.

sources.title: Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings
Ultra-high-density Neuropixels probes improve detection and identification in neuronal recordings

edges.label: needle-bed vs. shank sampling
edges.detail: The selected Utah design distributes projecting needles across a square base. NP 1.0 distributes sites along a narrow shank and integrates processing on the probe base.
edges.limit: Both access extracellular activity, but geometry, sampled tissue, electronics, and study context differ. This edge does not assert that Neuropixels descended from the Utah array.

sources.title: A glass/silicon composite intracortical electrode array
Fully integrated silicon probes for high-density recording of neural activity

edges.label: implements thin-film µECoG
edges.detail: The study uses subdural surface arrays. Its 1,024-channel design contains 977 recording-optimized, 42 stimulation-optimized, and 5 reference electrodes, connected to external headstages.
edges.limit: Micro-slit delivery evidence comes from porcine models and cadavers; human recordings in this paper were intraoperative. Do not present all 1,024 contacts as independent decoded neurons.

sources.title: Minimally invasive implantation of scalable high-density cortical microelectrode arrays for multimodal neural decoding and stimulation

edges.label: implements wireless CMOS µECoG
edges.detail: The authors describe a subdural cortical-surface device with electrodes and signal processing, telemetry, and wireless powering on one CMOS substrate.
edges.limit: The reported demonstrations are in pigs and non-human primates. This paper does not establish a chronic human BCI or 65,536 simultaneous recording channels.

sources.title: A wireless subdural-contained brain-computer interface with 65,536 electrodes and 1,024 channels

edges.label: cabled film vs. wireless chip
edges.detail: Both place electrodes at the cortical surface. Precision routes thin-film contacts to separate headstages; BISC integrates sensing and wireless electronics on its substrate.
edges.limit: Shared placement does not establish common ancestry, collaboration, or equal clinical readiness. Site count, recorded channels, reference contacts, coverage, and animal/human context must remain separate.

sources.title: Minimally invasive implantation of scalable high-density cortical microelectrode arrays for multimodal neural decoding and stimulation
A wireless subdural-contained brain-computer interface with 65,536 electrodes and 1,024 channels

edges.label: selectable-site CMOS architectures
edges.detail: Both use integrated electronics to read a selectable subset of physical electrode sites. NP 1.0 samples a penetrating shank; BISC samples the cortical surface wirelessly.
edges.limit: An architectural analogy, not demonstrated technological descent. It does not make their signals, power systems, sampling budgets, or neuron yields equivalent.

stories.title: Zhao, Xie & StairMed
stories.deck: A researcher’s path crosses institutions: Zhao’s UT Austin doctorate, work in Xie’s lab, a Rice postdoc, and co-founding StairMed. Select an entry to see the precise relationship and its dates.

stories.title: From NET to human recording
stories.deck: Follow explicitly cited fabrication methods from NET to MERF and human uFINE. StairMed’s hardware use is documented separately from the research lineage.

stories.title: Utah arrays & BrainGate
stories.deck: Follow development at Utah, the university’s documented technology license to Blackrock, and the use of arrays in BrainGate research. These are distinct roles in a larger system.

stories.title: Neuropixels branches
stories.deck: Progress branches. Neuropixels 2.0 miniaturizes the platform; Ultra uses the NP 1.0 platform for denser sampling. Compare their design goals without treating Ultra as a descendant of 2.0.

stories.title: Surface interfaces
stories.deck: Precision and BISC share cortical-surface sensing while integrating their electronics differently. Dashed links invite technical comparison; they do not assert common ancestry.

stories.title: A founder, two companies
stories.deck: A shared founder connects the companies; that does not establish a corporate spinout or inherited intellectual property.

stories.title: Rice lab → Motif
stories.deck: Rice explicitly describes Motif as a spinout of Robinson’s lab. This path carries miniature brain stimulation from a university laboratory into a company.

stories.title: The Synchron collaboration
stories.deck: The company emerged alongside a university laboratory and developed Stentrode with a multi-institution team.
